paras: The attempted lynching of the Hardin brothers took place at the jail in Fredonia, Kansas, in the night of 7-8 August 1881, when about forty armed and masked men tried to seize two brothers held for murder. The attack failed after the mob's leader, a farmer named John Hoffman, was shot at the cell door and killed, and the rest of the attackers fled. Papers across the country ran the story as a case of lynchers foiled, and several editorials used it as a lesson against lynch law.

The two brothers, named Hardin in nearly every report and 'Hayden' in one, were confined in the Fredonia jail awaiting trial for the murder of a man named Conner. Most accounts date that killing to 28 June, while the Stark County Democrat gives June 8, and the Saline County Journal described Conner as a farmer. No report gives the race of the brothers, of Conner or of the men who attacked the jail.

According to the dispatch from Fredonia dated 8 August, the masked men battered down the outer door of the jail and overpowered the two guards on duty. The Stark County Democrat added that they rode into town on horseback, followed by a wagon from which they took a crowbar and a heavy timber to break the door. Before being overpowered, one guard passed his pistol to a prisoner, and when Hoffman approached the cell with a crowbar, that prisoner fired and wounded him mortally.

The wire report said the mob put Hoffman in a wagon and fled, and that the sheriff raised a posse and went in pursuit. Hoffman was 'said' to have died soon afterward, and the wire described him as 'a well known farmer and much respected'. Later briefs spoke of the mob carrying off 'Hoffman's body', and the Watertown Republican called him 'a wealthy farmer'.

The Stark County Democrat reported that the sheriff's posse failed to overtake the attackers, and no report of arrests of mob members was found. On 30 September the Iola Register reported that the 'Harden murder case' of Wilson County would be tried at the next term of the Allen County court on a change of venue. The paper explained that public feeling against the brothers was too strong in Wilson County and recalled the recent attempt to lynch them.

The Fredonia dispatch reached dailies from Yankton and Sacramento to Savannah, Dallas, Chicago and Portland on 8 and 9 August, often in a crime roundup. Headline writers presented the result as a reversal for the mob: 'Lynchers Foiled' in Savannah and Chicago, 'A Mob Thwarted' in Dallas, 'Caught a Tartar' in St. Paul and 'Lynching a Lyncher' in the Daily Gazette. Shorter versions ran in weeklies through late August, including a syndicated brief that dated the attack 'the 7th inst.'.

Editorial comment, reprinted in the Emporia Weekly News, came from New York. The New York Tribune called mobs 'always cowardly' and said Kansas was 'a civilized state with courts, jails, and hangmen too', ending that 'Nobody was lynched, but one of the mob leaders was fatally wounded'. The New York Herald expected public sympathy to go to the prisoner who fired, but said those most deserving of lynching were communities that let their courts become 'too weak and slow to be trusted'. An editorial titled 'Western Lawlessness', printed in Marietta, Georgia, and Woodstock, Vermont, said the case 'shows the folly of lynch law' and that the mob 'were really about to commit murder'. None of this coverage mentioned race.

Accounts differ on who shot Hoffman. The widely printed wire report and the Somerset Press say a prisoner fired with a guard's pistol, while the Stark County Democrat says one guard fired and killed Hoffman as the other passed his revolver to the prisoners. The Saline County Journal, in Kansas, credited the two guards with a 'desperate resistance' that killed one lyncher and drove the others off. The Stark County Democrat also had the mob dispersing when townspeople gathered in large numbers, rather than fleeing with Hoffman in a wagon.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of the Hardin brothers, Fredonia, Kansas
bases: About forty armed, masked men attacked the Fredonia jail 'for the purpose of lynching' two brothers held for murder and were driven off (A4, A13, A14).

A band of about forty men tried to take two brothers accused of murder from jail to lynch them, but the brothers were not harmed; the only death was the mob's leader, shot by a defender (A4, A13, A23).

The wire report (A4, A8), a separately written version in the Stark County Democrat (A13) and a Kansas brief (A14) agree that the jail was attacked and the leader killed, though they differ on who fired; a Kansas paper later confirmed the attempt (A30).
